The Gaussian identity and what other neighbours change

Source: vignettes/theory-and-limits.Rmd
theory-and-limits.Rmd

The reference calculations assume jointly Gaussian responses, known mean and covariance, and fixed training locations, target weights and CV folds chosen independently of responses. They average over repeated response datasets at those locations. They do not equate an individual observed CV score with target MSE.

Prediction using one neighbour

Let the total response variance be VV and correlation with the nearest available training response be ρ(d)\rho(d). With known mean μ\mu, the Gaussian conditional mean based on that response Y1Y_1 is

Ŷ(t)=μ+ρ(d)(Y1−μ).\widehat Y(t)=\mu+\rho(d)(Y_1-\mu).

Its MSE is the conditional variance, V{1−ρ(d)2}V\{1-\rho(d)^2\}. Averaging separately over target and validation locations and subtracting gives

O1=RQ−C=V[ECρ(DC)2−EQρ(DQ)2]=VJ2.O_1=R_Q-C=V\left[\mathrm{E}_C\rho(D_C)^2-\mathrm{E}_Q\rho(D_Q)^2\right]=VJ_2.

Therefore minimising |J2||J_2| minimises absolute expected CV bias in this model. It does not minimise prediction MSE itself.

Prediction using all observations

Let e(t,T)e(t,T) be the MSE reduction from conditioning on all training responses in TT. The other observations provide the additional reduction

a(t,T)=e(t,T)−Vρ[D(t,T)]2≥0.a(t,T)=e(t,T)-V\rho[D(t,T)]^2\geq0.

The full difference is

Ofull=VJ2+a¯C−EQa(t,S).O_{\mathrm{full}}=VJ_2+\overline a_C-\mathrm{E}_Q a(t,S).

The final two terms compare the benefits of the other neighbours during validation and at the target. They need not cancel, and can change which CV scheme has the smallest absolute bias.

Reproduce the paper’s counterexample 

training <- cbind(c(-1, 0, 1), 0)
target <- prediction_target(matrix(c(2, 0), nrow = 1))
model <- spatial_covariance(range = 1, signal = 0.8, variance = 1)
folds <- cv_folds(1:3, n = 3)

audit_cv(training, folds, target, model)
#> Spatial CV audit
#>             A             W            J1            J2            U1 
#>  0.000000e+00  0.000000e+00  0.000000e+00 -1.387779e-17  0.000000e+00 
#>            U2 
#>  0.000000e+00 
#> Diagnostics compare prediction conditions; they do not certify CV accuracy.
result <- gaussian_cv(training, folds, target, model)
result
#> Gaussian reference calculation
#>            target_mse                cv_mse              optimism 
#>           0.912868743           0.889812660           0.023056082 
#>         one_neighbour additional_neighbours                 lower 
#>           0.000000000           0.023056082          -0.002661682 
#>                 upper 
#>           0.116354041

Every nearest-training distance is one, so W and J2 are zero. Nevertheless, target MSE exceeds expected CV MSE by approximately 0.02306. All of this difference comes from additional_neighbours.

When the observation at zero is held out, training observations lie one unit away on both sides. At the target location two, the training observations lie one, two and three units away, all on the same side. Matching only the closest distance omits this difference in available information.

result$validation[, c("nearest", "additional", "bound")]
#>      nearest   additional       bound
#> 1 0.08661458 0.0005133434 0.002344402
#> 2 0.08661458 0.0696915894 0.344373320
#> 3 0.08661458 0.0005133434 0.002344402
result$target[, c("nearest", "additional", "bound")]
#>      nearest   additional       bound
#> 1 0.08661458 0.0005166762 0.002661682

Bound the contribution

With independent observation noise variance τ2>0\tau^2>0, write b̃R\widetilde b_R for the remaining observations’ target covariances after removing their association through the nearest observation. If the spatial variance is σ2\sigma^2, the additional reduction satisfies

0≤a(t,T)≤B(t,T)=min⁡{∥b̃R∥2τ2,σ2−b12V}.0\leq a(t,T)\leq B(t,T)=\min\left\{ \frac{\|\widetilde b_R\|^2}{\tau^2},\ \sigma^2-\frac{b_1^2}{V}\right\}.

Consequently,

VJ2−EQB(t,S)≤Ofull≤VJ2+B¯C.VJ_2-\mathrm{E}_Q B(t,S)\leq O_{\mathrm{full}}\leq VJ_2+\overline B_C.

c(lower = result$lower, optimism = result$optimism, upper = result$upper)
#>        lower     optimism        upper 
#> -0.002661682  0.023056082  0.116354041

A positive lower bound guarantees underestimation of target MSE on average under the specified model. A negative upper bound guarantees overestimation. An interval containing zero does not establish a direction. These are deterministic bounds, not confidence intervals; they can be wide and require more covariance information than nearest distances alone. The complete proof is in the paper’s supplementary material.

Conditional MSE for an observed training dataset

Conditional on training responses, the MSE of an arbitrary supplied prediction is

Var⁡(Y(t)∣YS)+{E(Y(t)∣YS)−Ŷ(t)}2.\operatorname{Var}(Y(t)\mid Y_S) +\{\mathrm{E}(Y(t)\mid Y_S)-\widehat Y(t)\}^2.

Only when the prediction equals the conditional mean does MSE equal conditional variance. The following reference calculation makes the distinction explicit:

y <- c(0.2, -0.1, 0.5)
optimal <- gaussian_target_mse(training, y, target, model)
shifted <- gaussian_target_mse(training, y, target, model,
                              predictions = optimal$conditional_mean + 0.5)
c(conditional_mean_prediction = optimal$mse,
  shifted_prediction = shifted$mse,
  increase = shifted$mse - optimal$mse)
#> conditional_mean_prediction          shifted_prediction 
#>                   0.9128687                   1.1628687 
#>                    increase 
#>                   0.2500000

The increase is 0.52=0.250.5^2=0.25. In simulations the generating distribution is known. For real observations, replacing it with an estimated covariance gives a model-based calculation, not an exact measurement of prediction error.
